dossiers.label: Philosophy as practice for dying
dossiers.about: Those who rightly pursue philosophy practise nothing but dying and being dead: the separation of soul from body, which the philosopher seeks all his life; why then be vexed when it comes?

parts.label: Those who practise philosophy rightly practise dying
Death the release of soul from body
parts.quote: τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος ἀπαλλαγήν

parts.label: The practice of philosophers is this release
parts.quote: τὸ μελέτημα αὐτὸ τοῦτό ἐστιν τῶν φιλοσόφων

parts.label: Many bear the thyrsus, few are Bacchants

echoes.why: Taken up in the affinity argument: the pure soul has been practising death.

dossiers.label: Recollection in the Phaedo: the equal itself
dossiers.about: Cebes recalls Socrates' saying that learning is recollection. Equal sticks and stones seen fall short of the equal itself; we must have known the equal before we saw them, so the soul existed before birth.

passage.start_quote: ὅτι ἡμῖν ἡ μάθησις οὐκ ἄλλο τι ἢ ἀνάμνησις τυγχάνει οὖσα

parts.label: Learning is nothing but recollection
parts.quote: ἡ μάθησις οὐκ ἄλλο τι ἢ ἀνάμνησις

parts.label: The equal itself, beyond equal sticks and stones
They fall short of it
So our souls existed before birth, if these things are
parts.quote: τὸ ὁμοίως εἶναι τήν τε ψυχὴν ἡμῶν πρὶν γενέσθαι ἡμᾶς καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν

echoes.quote: τὸ γὰρ ζητεῖν ἄρα καὶ τὸ μανθάνειν ἀνάμνησις ὅλον ἐστίν
echoes.why: The Meno: all searching and learning is recollection.

echoes.quote: τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶν ἀνάμνησις ἐκείνων ἅ ποτʼ εἶδεν ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ
echoes.why: The Phaedrus: understanding is recollection of what the soul saw following a god.

related.why: Cebes cites the proof by questioning with diagrams, which the Meno shows.

dossiers.label: The swan song
dossiers.about: Socrates will not be thought a worse prophet than the swans, who sing most and best when they know they must die, not from grief but because they are Apollo's and foresee the good things in Hades.

passage.start_quote: τῶν κύκνων δοκῶ φαυλότερος ὑμῖν εἶναι τὴν μαντικήν
passage.end_quote: ἕως ἂν Ἀθηναίων ἐῶσιν ἄνδρες ἕνδεκα

parts.label: No worse a prophet than the swans
Apollo's birds, they foresee the good in Hades
parts.quote: τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος ὄντες, μαντικοί τέ εἰσι καὶ προειδότες τὰ ἐν Ἅιδου ἀγαθὰ

echoes.why: Socrates' death waited on the ship sent each year to Apollo at Delos.

dossiers.label: The second sailing
dossiers.about: Disappointed in Anaxagoras' Mind, which explained nothing by the best, Socrates takes 'the second voyage' in search of the cause: he takes refuge in logoi, lays down the strongest hypothesis, and posits beauty itself, the good itself and the rest.

parts.label: Anaxagoras' book: Mind orders all things
Socrates sits in prison not because of his bones and sinews
The second voyage in search of the cause
parts.quote: πλοῦν ἐπὶ τὴν τῆς αἰτίας ζήτησιν

parts.label: Not to look at the sun in an eclipse directly
Taking refuge in logoi
Laying down each time the strongest logos
parts.quote: ὑποθέμενος ἑκάστοτε λόγον ὃν ἂν κρίνω ἐρρωμενέστατον εἶναι

echoes.why: The 'safe and simple' cause that follows: by the beautiful all beautiful things are beautiful.
The divided line: the geometers proceed from hypotheses; dialectic goes up through them.

related.why: Hypothesis again, and the turn from looking at things directly to their images.

dossiers.label: The true earth (the Phaedo's myth)
dossiers.about: We live in a hollow of the earth like frogs round a pond, and take the murky air for heaven; the true earth above is like a ball of twelve coloured patches. Beneath, the rivers of the underworld, Ocean, Acheron, Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus, carry the dead to judgment.

passage.start_quote: εἴπερ ἡ ψυχὴ ἀθάνατος, ἐπιμελείας δὴ δεῖται
passage.end_quote: καλὸν γὰρ τὸ ἆθλον καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς μεγάλη

parts.label: If the soul is immortal, it needs care for all time
The earth is not as the geographers say
Like ants or frogs about a marsh
parts.quote: ὥσπερ περὶ τέλμα μύρμηκας ἢ βατράχους

parts.label: Like the twelve-patched balls
Tartarus and the rivers
Fair the prize, great the hope
parts.quote: καλὸν γὰρ τὸ ἆθλον καὶ ἡ ἐλπὶς μεγάλη

echoes.why: Socrates on the myth: no sensible man would insist it is just so, but it is a fine risk to believe it.

related.why: Another judgment myth, at the end of the Republic.
Our sea corrodes everything, as the waves have Glaucus.

dossiers.label: The death of Socrates
dossiers.about: Socrates bathes, sends away the women, drinks the hemlock calmly, walks until his legs are heavy, and his last words ask Crito to pay a cock to Asclepius. 'Such was the end of our friend, the best and wisest and most just.'

passage.start_quote: ταῦτ’ εἰπὼν ἐκεῖνος μὲν ἀνίστατο εἰς οἴκημά τι ὡς λουσόμενος

'We owe a cock to Asclepius'
The best, wisest and most just

echoes.why: The Apology's last words: now it is time to go, I to die, you to live; which is better, only the god knows.
The Crito: Crito at dawn in the prison, before the ship from Delos arrives.

related.why: The defence that brought him here.
